claim: Joining the loyalty program increased weekly sales at our stores.
context: 120 stores, weekly data for 16 weeks. 48 stores joined the loyalty program in week 9; the stores were picked by regional managers, not at random. Foot traffic is counted by door sensors every week. Loyalty sign-ups only exist for program stores.

reading.design_reason: The same 120 stores are seen every week before and after week 9, and only some of them joined the program. Managers chose the stores, so this is not an experiment; comparing each store's change over time with the change in stores that did not join (difference-in-differences) uses the before-period to absorb fixed differences between stores.

excluded.reason: Counted every week after the program started, so the program itself may change it. Adjusting for it would hide part of the effect.
Only exists for program stores and is a direct consequence of joining; it cannot be a cause of joining.
Free-text label with 97 distinct values; it carries no measured information beyond the store id.

draft_verdict.label: Supported
draft_verdict.sentence: Program stores grew weekly sales by about 2.9 thousand dollars more than other stores after joining, and the trends before week 9 look parallel.
reasons: Sales trends before week 9 do not differ clearly between program and other stores (e4).
A version with fewer covariates gives a similar number (e8).
assumed: Without the program, program stores would have followed the same sales trend as other stores (parallel trends after week 9).
No other change hit program stores at the same time as the program (no simultaneous shock).
Joining the program did not change sales at stores that did not join (no spillover).
Managers did not pick stores because of a sales change they saw coming (no anticipation).
No unmeasured factor drives both joining the program and sales (no hidden confounding).
caveats: Managers picked the stores, so they may have picked stores they expected to grow (e3).

judgments.why: Describes the table only: 1,920 rows, 120 stores by 16 weeks, no missing outcomes.
Treatment switches on within stores over time and never switches off, which is the layout a before/after comparison needs.
Program stores were about 18% larger and had higher sales before week 9; the comparison must rely on store-level differences staying fixed over time.
The test of differing trends before week 9 gives p = 0.41, so the before-period shows no clear gap in trends.
Eight weeks before the program is a short window; a trend test this short has little power to detect a slow divergence.
The estimate is positive (2.86) but the 95% interval runs from -0.41 to 6.12, so zero is not ruled out.
A hidden factor explaining about 4% of the remaining variation in both treatment and sales would be enough to bring the interval to zero; store size alone explains more than that.
The exploratory search links foot traffic and sales strongly, but foot traffic is measured after treatment and was left out; this says nothing about the claim.
Dropping region and baseline sales from the adjustment gives 2.71 with a similar interval, so the number does not hinge on those columns.

verdict.label: Inconclusive
verdict.sentence: The 95% interval for the effect runs from -0.41 to 6.12, so it includes zero. This data cannot show whether the program raised weekly sales, lowered them, or left them unchanged.
reasons: Sales trends before week 9 do not differ clearly between program and other stores (e4).
A version with fewer covariates gives a similar number (e8).
assumed: Without the program, program stores would have followed the same sales trend as other stores (parallel trends after week 9).
No other change hit program stores at the same time as the program (no simultaneous shock).
Joining the program did not change sales at stores that did not join (no spillover).
Managers did not pick stores because of a sales change they saw coming (no anticipation).
No unmeasured factor drives both joining the program and sales (no hidden confounding).
caveats: Managers picked the stores, so they may have picked stores they expected to grow (e3).
Only 8 weeks before the program are available to compare trends (e4).
A hidden factor about as strong as store size would be enough to move the interval to zero (e6).
Leaving out the first two program weeks gives a similar estimate whose interval also includes zero (e9).

violations.detail: The claim says the program increases weekly sales. Supported needs the 95% interval from e5 to lie entirely above zero, but it runs from -0.41 to 6.12.

args.question: Does the estimate change when weeks 9 and 10 (the first two program weeks) are left out?

lines: Method: two-way fixed effects (store and week), weeks 9 and 10 dropped, errors clustered by store.
Estimate 3.12, 95% interval -0.21 to 6.45 (t = 1.84, p = 0.068), on 1,680 rows.
With this spread, an effect of about 4.66 or larger would show up clearly.
Other specification tried: all weeks, estimate 2.86.
Limitation: dropping weeks shortens the post period from 8 to 6 weeks.

numbers.question: Does the estimate change when weeks 9 and 10 (the first two program weeks) are left out?
numbers.method: two-way fixed effects (store and week), weeks 9 and 10 dropped, errors clustered by store
limitations: Dropping weeks shortens the post period from 8 to 6 weeks.
numbers.code:
import json
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
out = {"question": "Does the estimate change when weeks 9 and 10 (the first two program weeks) are left out?",
       "method": "two-way fixed effects (store and week), weeks 9 and 10 dropped, errors clustered by store"}
try:
    d = df[~df["week"].isin([9, 10])]
    fit = smf.ols("weekly_sales ~ in_program + C(store_id) + C(week)", data=d).fit(
        cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": d["store_id"]})
    b, se = fit.params["in_program"], fit.bse["in_program"]
    lo, hi = fit.conf_int().loc["in_program"]
    full = smf.ols("weekly_sales ~ in_program + C(store_id) + C(week)", data=df).fit(
        cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["store_id"]})
    out.update({"statistic": float(fit.tvalues["in_program"]), "estimate": float(b), "std_error": float(se),
                "ci95_low": float(lo), "ci95_high": float(hi), "p_value": float(fit.pvalues["in_program"]),
                "n": int(len(d)), "detectable": float(2.8 * se),
                "alternatives": [{"spec": "all weeks", "estimate": float(full.params["in_program"])}],
                "limitations": ["Dropping weeks shortens the post period from 8 to 6 weeks."], "error": None})
except Exception as exc:
    out["error"] = str(exc)
with open("result.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(out, f)
